byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: The census of 1971 counted 548 million people, and fewer than one in three of them could read.

items.title: Population
items.summary: India's population was about 546 million in 1970; the census of March 1971 counted 547.9 million.

sources.label: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A newborn in 1970 could expect to live about 49 years.

items.title: Who could read
items.summary: At the 1971 census 29 to 34 percent of people could read and write, 39 to 46 percent of men and 19 to 22 percent of women.

items.title: Town and village
items.summary: About 20 percent of Indians lived in towns and cities.

gettingAround.standfirst: A scooter was something to wait years for.

items.summary: Official estimates in Delhi put the wait for a Vespa at about 5 years in 1963 and 11 years in 1966; by March 1970 pending bookings were reported at 176,933 for Vespa and Bajaj scooters and 84,883 for Lambrettas, and Parliament was told in 1973 that the waiting period was still long.

spotlight.title: The Green Revolution on the farm
spotlight.standfirst: After two droughts, new short-strawed wheat from Mexico and heavy use of fertiliser and irrigation raised India's foodgrain output by about a fifth between 1964-65 and 1970-71.

items.title: More grain
items.summary: Foodgrain production rose from 89 million tonnes in 1964-65 to almost 108 million tonnes in 1970-71.

sources.label: CIA Reading Room: India's foodgrain situation, progress and problems

items.title: Wheat before and after
items.summary: Wheat output was about 12.3 million tonnes in 1965 (11.4 million in 1966-67) and about 26.4 million tonnes by 1971-72, while yield per hectare rose to 1,380 kg from 663 in 1950-51.

sources.label: Review of Agrarian Studies (RAS): An eminent scientist and a great humanist
The Wire: Green Revolution, Borlaug and food security

items.title: Two failed monsoons
items.summary: Droughts in 1964-65 and 1965-66 caused food shortages, which pushed the adoption of new seed and fertiliser.

items.title: New wheat
items.summary: High-yielding, rust-resistant wheat varieties such as Kalyan Sona and Sonalika, bred by cross-breeding, were at the centre of the change, with the main gains in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

items.title: Mostly wheat
items.summary: The Green Revolution first provided more wheat; rice gains followed separately, and it depended heavily on irrigation.

sources.label: The Wire: Green Revolution, Borlaug and food security
CIA Reading Room: India's foodgrain situation, progress and problems

items.title: Punjab's share
items.summary: By 1970 Punjab was producing 70 percent of the country's food grains and farmers' incomes were reported to be rising by over 70 percent.
